title: The editor's headnote and the archive text
short: The archive prints Churton Collins's 1900 headnote and only the five opening Spenserian stanzas; the long 'Choric Song' that follows in Tennyson's poem is not included here.
body: This text comes from J. Churton Collins's annotated edition of Tennyson's early poems (1900). His headnote quotes the Odyssey passage (Book 9) in the Butcher and Lang prose version and lists the poets Tennyson borrowed from. The poem first came out in Poems (published December 1832, dated 1833) and was heavily revised for Poems (1842). In both versions these five narrative stanzas lead into an eight-part 'Choric Song' sung by the mariners. That song is missing from the archive text, which therefore ends just as the men begin to sing. Students should read the full poem in a standard edition such as Ricks's. In the full poem the two parts set narrative against lyric, and a shared epic action against the private wish of each man to give up.

title: 'Courage!' he said
short: The unnamed 'he' is Odysseus; the poem opens in mid-action with the leader's one word of resolve, which the rest of the poem quietly undoes.
body: Tennyson never names Odysseus. The leader's cry of 'Courage!' and his gesture toward land are all we hear from him, and it is the last firm act of will in the poem. Everything after it slows, softens and dissolves. In Homer the episode takes a few lines. Odysseus sends three men inland, they eat the lotus and forget their homecoming, and he drags them back weeping and ties them under the benches. Tennyson keeps the arrival and the eating but drops the rescue. The poem ends with the men's decision, not their leader's. Read beside 'Ulysses' (written 1833), where the aged hero again urges his mariners onward, the two poems make a pair: in one the will gives out, in the other it persists.

title: 'a land / In which it seemed always afternoon'
short: Time stops: the line turns the arrival hour into a permanent condition, and the repeated rhyme-word 'land' (ll. 1, 3) makes the stasis audible.
body: Line 3 ends 'unto a land', rhyming with 'toward the land' in line 1: Tennyson rhymes a word with itself, a small formal sign of a world where nothing moves on. The verb 'seemed' matters too. The poem keeps saying how things 'seem' (ll. 9, 24, 32, 35, 41), so the enchantment works on the men's perception before it works on their will. Critics often read the landscape as the outward form of a mood, a kind of Romantic 'indolence' like Keats's in his 'Ode on Indolence'.

title: 'seem' and the drugged perception
short: 'Seem' recurs throughout the stanzas: the lotos alters perception first, making the sea sound distant and voices 'thin', before it alters will.
body: Count the verbs of appearance: the stream 'did seem' to fall and pause (l. 9); 'all things always seem'd the same' (l. 24); the wave 'did seem to mourn and rave' (l. 32); the eater 'seem'd' asleep yet awake (l. 35); the sea 'Most weary seem'd' (l. 41). The narrative never says what the land is, only how it strikes the senses. This ties the descriptive stanzas to the drug. After the lotos, home and labour sound far off and the body's own heartbeat becomes 'music' (l. 36). Critics have linked this to Tennyson's lifelong interest in trance states. His Memoir reports his account of a waking trance he could bring on by repeating his own name.

title: 'like a downward smoke'
short: A waterfall so thin it seems to drift down like smoke; the simile is repeated at once, opening stanza 2.
body: The slender stream falls so lightly that it looks like smoke moving the wrong way, downward. The paradox matches the poem's slack, reversed energies. The phrase comes back in the opening line of stanza 2 ('A land of streams! some, like a downward smoke'), a repetition that copies the pause-and-fall movement of the water. Commentators have linked the mountain scenery here, as in 'Oenone', to the summer of 1830, when Tennyson and Arthur Hallam went to the Pyrenees to carry money to Spanish rebels. That link is general, and the poem's landscape is a composite. The next line turns the falling water into gauze or 'lawn' (l. 11).

title: lawn
greek: perhaps from Laon, French town of linen manufacture
short: Lawn: a very fine, sheer linen or cotton fabric; the streams fall like drifting veils.
body: 'Lawn' here is the cloth, not the grass: a fine, nearly transparent linen. The OED's suggested origin is the town of Laon in France, a centre of linen weaving. The metaphor turns the waterfalls into 'slow-dropping veils', delicate and slow. The next lines set this against streams that 'broke' through light and shadow into 'a slumbrous sheet of foam'. Even the violent water is drowsy ('slumbrous'). The veil image also prepares for the poem's interest in screening and half-seeing.

title: three mountain-tops ... of aged snow
short: Snow peaks flushed by sunset: a distant, untouchable sublime, set far beyond the soft valley of the lotos-land.
body: The view travels inland from the shore to 'three silent pinnacles of aged snow', lit red by the sunset. 'Aged' makes the snow ancient and permanent, outside the drowsy present of the valley. The mountains are silent, as the whole landscape is muffled. Some readers see Alpine or Pyrenean memory here; there is no snow-capped triple peak in Homer's brief episode, so this is Tennyson's addition. The scene is a painterly, Turner-like composition of moonlight, sunset and mist at once. The coexistence of sun and moon becomes explicit at l. 38.

title: Up-clomb
greek: Old English climban, past tense clamb
short: 'Clomb' is the old strong past tense of 'climb'; the pine 'climbed up' above the thicket.
body: 'Clomb' descends from the Old English strong verb climban (past clamb) and was already archaic in Tennyson's time. The OED records it surviving in dialect and poetry, notably in Milton (Paradise Lost 4.192, of Satan: 'So clomb this first grand thief into God's fold'). With the prefix 'Up-' it gives a deliberately antique, Spenserian colouring to the stanza. That suits a poem whose form and diction look back to The Faerie Queene. The 'woven copse' is a dense thicket whose branches interlace.

title: galingale
greek: Arabic khalanjān, via Old French galingal
short: A sedge, English galingale (Cyperus longus), with aromatic roots; the exotic name adds a scented, Eastern note to the meadow.
body: The word first named an aromatic root from the East (Alpinia, used as a spice), and only later the native English sedge Cyperus longus, whose root smells similar. Chaucer's Cook uses 'galyngale' as a spice in the General Prologue. Tennyson's 'slender galingale' is clearly a plant growing in the meadow, so the sedge is meant. The word's sound and Eastern origin still add perfume and remoteness. Ricks's notes discuss the word. Tennyson cared about naming plants exactly, and his botanical terms are rarely only decorative.

title: 'A land where all things always seem'd the same!'
short: The exclamation sums up the lotos-land: no change, no history, no future, which is both its charm and its threat.
body: The line is built from sameness: 'all', 'always', 'same', with alliterating l- and s- sounds. Change is what makes a journey, a story or a homecoming possible. A land without it offers rest, but also the end of the Odyssey's narrative of return (nostos). Victorian readers often read the poem as a debate about duty and withdrawal; for 1842 Tennyson added a Choric Song stanza on the wives and homes left behind and rewrote the last stanza around Lucretian gods careless of mankind. Critics disagree on how far Tennyson condemns the mariners. Some read the poem as moral warning; others, as a sympathetic statement of a real longing for rest.

title: the Lotos-eaters
short: Homer's Lotophagi, who offer strangers the honey-sweet lotos that makes them forget home; Herodotus placed them on the Libyan coast.
body: In Odyssey 9 the Lotus-eaters mean no harm: they simply share their food, and whoever tastes it forgets the way home. Herodotus (4.177) puts a people of this name on the coast of Libya and describes the lotus fruit as about the size of a mastic berry and as sweet as a date. Botanists often identify it with the jujube shrub Ziziphus lotus. Tennyson's eaters are 'mild-eyed' and 'melancholy', with 'dark faces pale' against the sunset. They are less tempters than living examples of what the mariners will become. The sadness is in them already.

title: Branches ... of that enchanted stem
short: The eaters offer branches laden with both flower and fruit at once, a sign of a magic season outside nature's order.
body: Flower and fruit together on one branch is an old mark of the earthly paradise or enchanted garden. Spenser's Garden of Adonis (Faerie Queene 3.6) has 'continuall spring, and haruest' at once. Homer's lotus is simply a 'flowery food'. Tennyson makes the gift ritual: 'whereof they gave / To each'. The syntax then spills over the line ending ('whoso did receive of them, / And taste'), so the reader slides into the effect as the eater does. Note the biblical cadence of 'whoso did receive of them'.

title: thin voices and the beating heart
short: After eating, the world goes faint and distant: a comrade's voice sounds ghostly, and the only music left is the eater's own heartbeat.
body: The drug turns attention inward. The sea seems to 'mourn and rave / On alien shores', so the real world is now foreign. A friend's voice is 'thin' like the voices of the dead; in Homer (Odyssey 11, and Iliad 23.101) the shades speak in thin, gibbering cries. The paradox 'deep-asleep he seem'd, yet all awake' describes a trance. The last line hands the poem's music over to the body: 'music in his ears his beating heart did make'. Some critics treat this as an image of the lyric poet's own self-absorption.

title: 'Between the sun and moon upon the shore'
short: The men sit between the setting sun and the rising full moon (l. 7): a border place, between day and night, sea and land.
body: Stanza 1 set a 'full-faced' moon above the valley, and stanza 3 a sunset 'linger'd low adown'. A full moon does rise as the sun sets, so the picture is accurate, but Tennyson uses it symbolically. The mariners sit on the shore between elements and times, neither at sea nor inland, neither working nor yet asleep. The yellow sand and yellow down repeat a golden palette. The line is the stillest in the poem, the moment before the decision.

title: Father-land ... child, and wife, and slave
short: Home becomes something sweet only 'to dream of', and the household list, ending in 'slave', recalls the Homeric oikos the men abandon.
body: 'Father-land', with its hyphen, translates the Greek idea of patris, the land of one's fathers. The list 'child, and wife, and slave' names the Homeric household (oikos), in which slaves were part of the family. Note that home is now an object of reverie, pleasant to dream of, not a goal. The adversative 'but evermore' turns at once to weariness, with 'weary' said three times (ll. 41-42). Penelope and Telemachus wait at the end of the epic; these men choose the dream over the return.

title: 'the wandering fields of barren foam'
short: The sea as fields that bear no crop: a version of Homer's stock epithet atrygetos, 'barren' or 'unharvested', for the sea.
body: Homer often calls the sea atrygetos, usually translated 'barren' or 'unharvested' (for instance Iliad 1.316). The epithet sets the sea against the fruitful ploughland. Tennyson turns it into a metaphor: the sea is a field, but 'wandering' and made of foam, so it yields nothing for all the rowing. The line closes the triple 'weary', then strikes the main theme: labour without harvest. The Choric Song (not printed here) develops the contrast between toiling men and resting nature.

anchor: to fall and pause and fall
title: Spenserian stanza and the long last line
short: Each stanza is Spenserian: eight pentameters and a closing alexandrine (six stresses) rhyming ababbcbcc; the long last line slows and settles.
body: Tennyson borrows the nine-line stanza of The Faerie Queene, rhymed ababbcbcc, whose final line has twelve syllables. Its length makes each stanza close with a long, sinking cadence, suited to drowsiness: 'Along the cliff to fall and pause and fall did seem'. The choice also announces his debts: Spenser's Idle Lake and Thomson's Castle of Indolence, itself in Spenserian stanzas, are the main English models for lands of seductive idleness. In the Choric Song (not printed here) Tennyson moves to irregular lines and rhymes, so the contrast of forms shapes the whole poem.

title: Spenser, Thomson, Moschus and Bion
short: Collins names Tennyson's main models: Spenser's Idle Lake (Faerie Queene 2.6), Thomson's Castle of Indolence, and idylls of Moschus and Bion.
body: In Faerie Queene 2.6 the wanton Phaedria ferries Guyon across the Idle Lake to an island of ease and idleness. In Thomson's Castle of Indolence (1748) the wizard Indolence lures pilgrims into a land of 'drowsy-head'. The short poems of the Greek bucolic poets Moschus (Idyll 5) and Bion (Idyll 5 in some numbering) contrast the toil of the sailor's life with the peace of the land. Collins, an energetic hunter of sources, documented such parallels at length; Tennyson disliked having his poems traced to sources in this way. Ricks's notes give a fuller, more cautious account.

title: 'We will return no more'
short: One unnamed man speaks the refusal and all sing it; the narrative ends here, giving way to the mariners' Choric Song.
body: 'Some one said' keeps the speaker anonymous: the decision becomes collective without anyone owning it. The men then sing together, 'Our island home / Is far beyond the wave'. Their island is Ithaca; 'home' is still theirs, but given up. Here the speaking voice shifts from the narrator to the chorus, and the full poem goes on to their song. Readers differ over whether Tennyson endorses the mariners' longing (a reading encouraged by the Choric Song's beauty) or exposes it as moral collapse (as many Victorian reviewers and the 1842 additions suggest). Many modern critics see the poem as holding both views in tension.
